newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists reaffirm commitment to reform.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists reaffirm commitment to reform.

text.p: Bulgaria's former ruling Socialists said on Tuesday they remained committed to an agreement between the interim cabinet and the International Monetary Fund despite reservations expressed by party leader Georgi Parvanov.
In a letter to President Petar Stoyanov published by Bulgarian newspapers on Monday, Parvanov complained of a lack of transparency and of politically motivated sackings of senior state employees.

"Our mutual desire is that the course of economic reform should continue and that the negotiations with international financial institutions should conclude successfully this week," Miroslav Popov, a member of the Socialist Party's executive bureau, said.
The Group of 24 industrialised nations are meeting in Brussels to discuss extra support for Bulgaria, and the standby accord goes to the International Monetary Fund board on Friday.

Popov told reporters after three hours of talks between Stoyanov and party leaders that the Socialists did not object to the IMF accord but wanted more transparency and dialogue from the interim cabinet.

"The president understands the concern of the Socialists that many directors of the state firms have been sacked and some former ministers and officials are not allowed to leave the country," Popov said.

Former agriculture minister Vassil Chichibaba and three of his deputies have been charged with complicity over their role in excessive grain exports in 1995, which created shortages that have persisted into this year.
The interior ministry said last month it had also submitted evidence implicating former prime minister Zhan Videnov and he had been temporarily barred from travelling abroad.
Some newspapers dismissed Parvanov's letter as a political ploy ahead of elections on April 19.
Interim prime minister Stefan Sofianski said on Tuesday the dismissals of managers were made for operational reasons and the need for reform was obvious from the state of the economy.
